n: Common Infectious Diseases in East Africa

faq.a: Artesunate reduces mortality and clears parasites faster with fewer cardiac side‑effects.
faq.q: Why give IV artesunate instead of quinine for severe malaria?

faq.a: If the patient is afebrile, haemodynamically stable and cultures are negative after 48‑72 h, de‑escalate according to guidelines.
faq.q: When can I stop antibiotics in sepsis?

faq.a: Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality and neurological sequelae in HIV‑negative adults.
faq.q: What is the role of steroids in TB meningitis?

exam: A 28‑year‑old with fever, chills every 48 h and splenomegaly – what is the most likely diagnosis and first test? — Malaria; perform rapid malaria test.

A patient with chronic cough, weight loss, and a chest X‑ray showing cavitation – which investigation confirms the cause and what is the initial regimen? — Sputum smear or GeneXpert for TB; start 2‑month intensive phase with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol.

In a febrile child with diarrhoea, how do you differentiate cholera from typhoid without stool culture? — Look for profuse watery stools, dehydration, and rice‑water appearance for cholera; typhoid shows stepwise fever and abdominal pain.
A HIV‑positive patient presents with fever, night sweats, and a negative sputum smear – what is your next step? — Consider GeneXpert or treat empirically for TB if high clinical suspicion.
Why avoid fluoroquinolones in a patient with QT prolongation? — They can exacerbate arrhythmias; choose macrolides or beta‑lactams instead.
What are the red‑flag signs of severe malaria that mandate referral? — Altered consciousness, respiratory distress, renal failure, severe anaemia (<5 g/dL).
How would you manage sepsis in a setting without blood culture facilities? — Give broad‑spectrum antibiotics promptly, fluid resuscitation, and monitor vitals; obtain cultures when possible later.
When is it safe to discharge a patient after completing TB treatment? — After 6 months of therapy with documented sputum conversion and clinical improvement.
ai.title: Common Infectious Diseases in East Africa
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A clinician‑focused overview of the most frequent infections seen in low‑resource East African hospitals, their presentation, bedside assessment, essential investigations and pragmatic management.

b: Use a focused history (travel, exposure, immunisation, HIV status).
Perform a targeted physical exam to localise infection.
sections.p: Infectious diseases are illnesses caused by pathogenic microorganisms that can be identified by clinical patterns, epidemiology and limited laboratory tests.

t.b: Is the patient infected with Plasmodium? Positive line = malaria; negative does not rule out low‑parasitaemia.
Is pulmonary TB present? Positive = TB; if unavailable, treat empirically when high suspicion.
Is the patient HIV positive? Positive = HIV infection; if unavailable, use clinical staging.

b: Malaria: uncomplicated vs severe (cerebral signs, respiratory distress, renal failure).
TB: uncomplicated pulmonary vs disseminated/miliary.
Sepsis: qSOFA ≥2 indicates high risk.
sections.p: Severity guides urgency of treatment and level of care.

b: Fever: malaria, bacterial sepsis, typhoid, HIV‑related infections.
Respiratory cough: TB, bacterial pneumonia, viral influenza.
Diarrhoea: cholera, shigella, cryptosporidium, HIV‑related opportunists.
sections.p: In this region the common aetiologies cluster by organ system.

b: Malaria – cyclic fever, chills, headache, splenomegaly.
Pulmonary TB – chronic cough >2 weeks, night sweats, weight loss.
Typhoid – stepwise fever, abdominal pain, rose spots.
sections.p: Typical patterns help narrow the differential.
Prioritise bedside and low‑cost tests; use alternatives when unavailable.

t.b: Is there anaemia or leukocytosis? Low Hb suggests malaria or chronic disease; neutrophilia points to bacterial infection.
Is there protein or haematuria? May indicate schistosomiasis or severe malaria renal involvement.
Is there infiltrate or cavitation? Infiltrate = pneumonia; cavitation = TB.

b: Altered mental status – cerebral malaria or meningitis.
Persistent vomiting, oliguria – severe malaria renal failure.
Weight loss >10 % + night sweats – disseminated TB.
Malaria – IV artesunate for severe disease; oral ACT for uncomplicated.
TB – 2‑month intensive phase (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) then continuation phase; avoid fluoroquinolones if QT prolongation risk.
Sepsis – early broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) after cultures; give IV fluids 30 ml/kg if hypotensive.
sections.p: Treat the pathogen first, then support organ function.

b: Malaria – repeat RDT after 48 h if fever persists; insecticide‑treated nets.
TB – sputum smear at 2 months and end of treatment; directly observed therapy.
Vaccination – hepatitis B, pneumococcal, typhoid where available.
Malaria vs viral fever – malaria has periodic chills and splenomegaly.
TB vs bacterial pneumonia – TB is more chronic, weight loss prominent.
Typhoid vs malaria – typhoid lacks cyclic fever and splenomegaly.
Malaria RDT may be negative in low‑parasitaemia; smear remains gold standard.
Sputum smear can miss early TB; consider GeneXpert if available.
HIV rapid test window period up to 4 weeks; repeat if high risk.
sections.p: Be aware of false negatives and atypical patterns.
